messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 51
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Doctor
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Body Parts): Specific body parts associated with the event, Authority Presence: Police, Offender Cues: Seeing the offender
  Maladaptive Strategies: Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement, Concealing Clothing: wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed, Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
  Threat: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Linh Nguyen is a 51-year-old physician who came to treatment months after an assault that still felt, in her words, “impossible and yet always right beside me.” She is a married Vietnamese American doctor, and before the assault she had moved through hospitals and clinics with the practiced confidence of someone long accustomed to pressure, hierarchy, and human vulnerability. What happened to her occurred after work, when she was confronted and assaulted by a man whose face and physical presence she can still identify immediately. In the moments that stand out most sharply, she remembers fragments with an almost punishing clarity: the sight of his body at close range, the proximity of particular body parts that now act as instant reminders, the smell present at the scene that returns to her unexpectedly when she thinks about it, and the abrupt, engulfing terror that made the world feel at once vivid and unreal. When she tries to describe the event in sequence, she often falters and says it feels like a story about someone else, too extreme to have happened to her, yet when any part of it is stirred she is back inside the same fear.

In the weeks afterward, Linh found that reminders were not abstract. They appeared in ordinary life with a force that stunned her. Seeing a man in public whose build or posture resembled the offender could make her heart lurch before she had fully registered why. More specifically, glimpses of certain male body parts associated with the assault could make her freeze internally, look away, and feel the air leave the room. She was especially shaken by the presence of police. Even when an officer was simply standing near the hospital entrance or speaking to staff in a neutral way, she felt her body tense. The authority of the uniform did not reassure her; it became part of the network of cues around what had happened. She could not pass these moments off as simple discomfort. What frightened her most was how completely they seemed to take over, bringing with them not just memory but the same terror.

As a doctor, she could not avoid exposure to bodies or strangers. In the hospital, routine examinations became fraught in private ways she tried hard not to show. She remained outwardly competent, but internally she was bracing herself through encounters that had once been unremarkable. Unexpected noises on the ward—a metal tray dropped, a door pushed open too hard, a monitor alarm sounding sharply—sent her into instant high alert. Silence was no better. If a corridor suddenly went quiet late in the day, or if she found herself alone in an exam room between patients, the stillness itself began to feel dangerous, as though something bad was about to break through it. She also became wary of strangers approaching her, even in ordinary situations like walking from the parking structure or standing in line for coffee in the hospital lobby. Her mind no longer granted everyday safety automatically. She had come to believe that the basic rules she once trusted—that professionalism, decency, and the ordinary structure of life offered some protection—had been destroyed.

At home and at work, Linh began organizing her life around not being noticed and not being reminded. She started wearing loose, concealing clothing, choosing outfits that hid her shape and made her feel less visible. She avoided any cues linked to the perpetrator, changing routes and leaving places quickly if someone looked like him. If thoughts about the assault surfaced, she pushed them away with urgency because she was certain that if she let herself think too much about it, she would not be able to handle what came next. This avoidance narrowed her world over time. Her husband noticed that outings became shorter and more conditional, and that she scanned rooms before sitting down. She did not tell him everything; part of her no longer trusted people in the way she once had, and part of her could not bear to make the event feel more real by speaking it fully.

One habit that developed in the months after the assault alarmed her enough that she eventually mentioned it in treatment: she had started gambling for distraction and for the jolt of excitement. The bright, absorbing intensity gave her temporary relief from the deadened dread and vigilance that otherwise filled so much of her day. It was not consistent with how she had known herself before, and she felt ashamed of the secrecy around it.

By the time she sought help, Linh was exhausted by the effort of living like this while continuing to work as a physician. The immediate reason was a recent series of incidents at the hospital: seeing a police officer near the emergency department, hearing a sudden crash behind her, and then catching sight of a man who resembled the offender had left her shaken for hours. She went home and told her husband that she could no longer keep pretending this was passing. What she fears most is that if she allows herself to face the assault directly, the terror will overwhelm her completely. What she hopes, more quietly, is that life might stop feeling organized around danger, and that she might one day move through her work, her marriage, and her own body without expecting threat in every silence.
